q6.answer: A must stop itself. A watchdog on A's primary may take writes only while it renews a short lease (about 15 s) in the external record store. The FAILING_OVER write makes renewal impossible, and a store outage makes it fail too. So the watchdog fast-shuts-down A's PostgreSQL about 15 s after its last successful renewal, using its own monotonic clock. The command waits until the lease expiry plus a skew margin (proposed 5 s) before promoting B. The wait is only a timer. A frozen watchdog is the residual risk.

q7.answer: A small active-region record in a strongly consistent store outside both regions, with compare-and-set and multi-key transactions. It holds {active_region, epoch, state, step, run_id}. The failover command reads it in the pre-checks and writes it at FAILING_OVER, at each step and at ACTIVE. A's watchdog does not read the record directly. It renews a separate lease key in a transaction that checks the record still says A is active at its epoch. The product is not chosen.

q8.answer: After B's database is promoted and before any worker starts, the command resets every `running` row in B's `jobs` table to `queued`. B has no workers yet, so all of those rows are orphans. A job may have finished in A with side effects while its completion never reached B, so it can run twice. Handlers therefore need to be idempotent. Stale A workers cannot mark anything done because A's database is stopped. Jobs A committed after the last WAL receipt are lost. The command prints a summary but cannot list them.

q9.answer: Resume works by rerunning the command with `--resume` from any host, after the person confirms the earlier command has stopped. It reads run_id and step from the FAILING_OVER record. The step says where to start, but each step checks real state first and skips itself if done, and real state wins on disagreement. After the failed run's retries are exhausted, the person escalates to the secondary on-call. Going back to A is only possible before the FAILING_OVER write, when nothing has changed and you simply start again later. After that write, A has stopped itself, so backing out is a manual human decision that needs un-fencing. The default is to resume forward, and after promotion it only goes forward.

q10.answer: I did not model client-side behaviour in detail. Resolvers may keep serving A's address for up to 60 s after DNS moves, because of the TTL. During the failover, and until DNS moves, A's app tier is untouched but gets database errors once A's database is stopped, so those users see errors. A's database stays stopped, so nothing can be written there. Every user must sign in again on B because B's Redis is empty. I did not decide whether A's app should redirect or serve a maintenance page.

q11.answer: Up to the replay lag recorded at the last WAL receipt (typically under 5 s, RPO target 30 s), plus anything A committed after that last receipt, which is unmeasured. Asynchronous replication is the cause. The command stops if the recorded lag is over 30 s, unless the person passes an explicit accept-data-loss override. The check does not guarantee RPO, because the recorded value does not grow while A is down. The command prints the time of the last WAL receipt so on-call can judge the gap.
